class.name: NetwParticipant
class.brief_description: Live handle for one accepted session player.
class.description: A view over one peer's row in the session, holding nothing but the peer id: every member is read back through the session when it is asked for, so a participant is correct after a rehost, a scene rebuild or a respawn without anything re-issuing it. One peer has one participant, so [code]==[/code] answers "the same player". [member current_scene] tracks the peer's primary scene independently of any spawned player node, which is what lets a session seat a player before it has a body and keep the seat after the body is gone. [codeblock] var participant := api.peer_get_participant(peer_id) if participant.identity: greet(participant.username) await participant.move_to(arena).completed [/codeblock] Minted by the session and never by a caller: [method NetwMultiplayer.peer_get_participant] mints the row the first time a peer is asked about, so two reads of one peer answer the same object.

method.name: move_to
method.description: Travels this participant into [param destination]: the player entity roots it is enrolled in move first, then its admission and its [member current_scene] follow. This is the whole of arriving rather than the membership half of it, which is why it answers a promise. Admissions this participant holds elsewhere are untouched, so a spectator seat survives travel. A move into the scene already held is a successful no-op raising no roster event. The returned [NetwPromise] resolves once the transfer has committed on authority. It rejects with [constant @GlobalScope.ERR_BUSY] while another transfer of the same participant is in flight, with [constant @GlobalScope.ERR_UNAVAILABLE] when [param destination] retired while the transfer was preparing, and with [constant @GlobalScope.ERR_UNAUTHORIZED] off authority. A client never calls this. It asks through [method Netw.change_scene_to_file] at [constant Netw.SCENE_CHANGE_PARTICIPANT], and the server derives which participant is asking from the authenticated connection rather than from anything the client sent. To change which scene a participant belongs to without moving their node, use [method NetwMultiplayer.scene_admit] and [method NetwMultiplayer.scene_release]. [b]Server Only.[/b]

members.member: The typed join arguments accepted for this peer. See [member ResolvedJoin.arg_values].

The scene this peer counts as being in, or [code]null[/code] outside every scene. Primary, not exclusive: a participant may be admitted to several scenes at once, and this names the one that places it and drives its default presentation. Admitting a participant somewhere else does not move this, and travel does. Read-only, because writing it would record arrival without performing it. [method move_to] is the verb that actually moves a participant, and the deliberate low-level seat verbs on [NetwMultiplayer] are there for a caller managing membership without moving anything. The seat is held as the scene entity's identity rather than as a handle, so membership survives the scene being rebuilt and never pins a freed node; the handle read here is minted from that identity on demand.

The validated auth identity for this peer, or [code]null[/code]. Present only when the session has an auth provider, and never part of the replicated roster, which is what [ResolvedJoin] is. Read from the session's own book through [method NetwMultiplayer.peer_get_identity], which is the one answer to who authenticated.

The accepted join record for this peer, or [code]null[/code] before the join is accepted. Read through [method NetwMultiplayer.peer_get_accepted_join] on every access rather than held, so a join enriched after the participant was minted is answered by the participant that already exists.
The peer this participant represents. The one piece of state it holds, because everything else is a read.
The accepted username for this peer, empty before the join is accepted. See [member ResolvedJoin.username].

signal.name: scene_changed
signal.description: Emitted when [member current_scene] changes, carrying the [NetwSceneHandle] left and the one arrived in, either of which may be [code]null[/code]. Emitted by the seat verbs themselves rather than by whoever called them, so a seat written by a move, by a release and by a session teardown all announce the same way. A silent write is the failure this closes: a seat that changed without announcing leaves every viewer showing the previous scene. The session republishes the local participant's edge as [signal NetwMultiplayer.scene_local_changed], rebinding it as the local row comes and goes, so a game that only cares about this peer listens there and never has to hold a participant to do it.
